description:
Hi! I'm Aml, a Computer Science student specializing in Cybersecurity at SUT. I'm passionate about technology, space, and innovation, and I previously won 2nd place in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2022.

I'm looking for creative, motivated teammates skilled in programming, design, 3D modeling, or storytelling to turn forgotten space equipment into engaging stories.
summary:
BeyondX is an interactive space museum that brings the stories of humanity's forgotten space explorers back to life. We developed an immersive website where users can explore three environments: the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space, discovering the spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific equipment left behind.
Each artifact has its interactive experience, providing visitors with information about its identity, purpose, mission, and scientific contributions, supported by engaging voice-over narration.
To make space exploration accessible to different audiences, BeyondX features two experiences: Kids Mode, which presents information through simple, fun, and engaging storytelling, and Adult Mode, which offers a more detailed educational experience.
Our project directly addresses NASA's challenge, *"Abandoned but not Forgotten,"* by transforming historical mission information into an interactive storytelling experience rather than simply presenting technical facts. It helps users understand not only what equipment was left behind, but also why it was sent, what it accomplished, and how it contributed to our understanding of the universe.
BeyondX is important because these forgotten machines represent decades of human curiosity, innovation, and scientific achievement. By preserving their stories in an accessible and engaging digital museum, we aim to inspire the next generation, encourage curiosity about space, and remind everyone that even when a mission ends, its legacy lives on.
details:
BEYONDX

Some missions end. Their stories remain.

What exactly does it do?

BEYONDX is an interactive 3D web experience that turns the equipment humanity left behind in space into stories anyone can explore. Instead of reading a list of missions, the user travels to a world, lands on its surface, and discovers each object for themselves.

The experience has three collections and 29 independent stories:

Moon (16 stories): the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage, the three Lunar Roving Vehicles, the five ALSEP science stations, and the seven Surveyor landers, including the two that crashed.

Mars (8 stories): Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, and the Ingenuity helicopter, plus a timeline showing how each generation asked a new question about Mars.

Deep Space (5 stories): Pioneer 10, Pioneer 11, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, and the Kepler Space Telescope.

Every story answers the same six questions: What was it? Why was it sent? What did it do? What did it discover? What happened to it? Why does it still matter?

How does it work?

The user chooses a world from the Space Hub and watches a cinematic descent to its surface.

Glowing markers show where equipment is waiting. There is no fixed order; the user picks any marker.

The camera flies to the object, which first appears only as a dark silhouette.

The user is asked “What do you think this is?” with three choices (or can skip).

The object is revealed as a 3D model, and its story unfolds step by step while the relevant part of the model lights up.

The story ends with the object’s final fate: a timeline, key facts, its real coordinates, and NASA sources.

A single switch turns on Kids Mode. The facts stay exactly the same, but the whole experience changes: simpler language, a friendly astronaut guide named Cosmo who reacts to the child’s answers, star-based progress, confetti for correct guesses, and a quiz with a certificate. Each story also has recorded narration in both a Kids and an Adults version.

What benefits does it have?

Makes space history accessible. Complex missions become short, clear stories that need no prior knowledge.

Serves two audiences with one product. Adults get a documentary-style experience with dates, instruments and sources; children get an adventure built on the same facts.

Learning by discovery. Guessing before the reveal makes users curious and helps them remember what they learn.

Scientific honesty. We separate launch, landing, last contact and official mission end; we never present life on Mars as proven; and we clearly label our 3D terrain and models as illustrative reconstructions while showing the real coordinates as text.

Easy to extend. Stories are stored as data, separate from the interface, so new missions can be added without rebuilding the site.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want people to see these objects not as abandoned machines but as part of humanity’s history. Our goals are to preserve the stories behind the hardware, to give teachers and families a tool that works for both adults and children, and to inspire the next generation of explorers. In the future we hope to add more missions, real NASA imagery and terrain data, and more languages.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS, GLSL (procedural noise for terrain and textures)

Framework and build: React, Vite

3D graphics: Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei. All spacecraft models and both planetary surfaces are generated procedurally in code.

Animation: GSAP (cinematic camera movement), Motion (interface transitions)

State management: Zustand

Styling: Tailwind CSS

Audio: recorded narration for every story group in Kids and Adults versions, plus Web Audio for small interface sounds

Data and references: NASA, NASA Science, NASA JPL, and the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA)

Hardware: none required. It runs in any modern web browser on desktop or mobile.
